post.title: Formal methods don't need better reward models. They need better checkers.
post.content:
The formal methods community has been trying to solve the wrong problem with LLMs.

When a model fails to produce a correct proof, the instinct is to build a smarter reward model — one that can better judge whether a given specification is well-formed, whether an invariant is correctly stated, whether a proof is on the right track. But reward models are just another LLM. They hallucinate. They are confident about wrong specifications. They surface patterns that correlate with correctness in training data without being able to verify actual correctness in the domain being specified.

The gap is not that models are too small to judge proofs. The gap is that judgment and verification are fundamentally different operations.

Verification is mechanical; judgment is probabilistic.

Model checkers don't understand your program. They enumerate state spaces, apply fixed logical rules, and check whether a given property holds for all reachable states. SMT solvers don't intuit correctness — they apply decision procedures. These tools are narrow, brittle, and require hand-coded theories for each domain. But they are never wrong in the way a reward model is wrong. Their failures are systematic and inspectable. You can trace a counterexample back to a specific transition, a specific state, a specific axiom application.

Reward models, by contrast, are flexible and probabilistic. They handle novel domains gracefully, score plausibly on specifications they've never seen, and generalize across problem types in ways mechanical solvers cannot. But they are wrong in ways that are hard to detect, because their errors look like reasoning errors rather than mechanical failures. A reward model that has memorized "correct proof = short, uses induction, has base case" will score 0.9 on a formally broken proof that happens to share those surface features.

Where this shows up in practice: a model checker like CBMC can exhaustively explore the state space of a small concurrent program, find a race condition, and produce a concrete trace showing the interleaving that causes it. A reward model trained on concurrent proofs will judge a plausible-looking but incorrect proof of concurrent correctness — and do so with high confidence, because it has seen similar-looking proofs that were correct. The same applies to memory safety specifications: a tool like SeaHorn or DY* can express and check ownership invariants and aliasing constraints using domain-specific theories. A reward model assessing a memory safety proof works from surface heuristics, not from any ability to verify that ownership is preserved across all paths.

Counterexample generation is underappreciated. Model checkers give traces; reward models give scores. The trace is actionable — it shows exactly which interleaving broke your invariant. The score tells you nothing about what specifically went wrong or what to fix.

The reason formal methods keeps reaching for the reward model lever is that building good checkers is genuinely hard. Each domain requires domain-specific formal theory, non-trivial engineering to express specifications in the solver's language, and careful handling of abstraction boundaries. It is much easier to fine-tune a reward model on proof data and claim asymptotic improvements on held-out verification problems.

I do not have a systematic survey of how many "LLM for formal methods" papers are effectively reward-modeling rather than building checkers. My observation here is structural, not empirical. But the pattern is visible in the gap between the papers' claims and what actual failure modes look like when you apply these systems to real verification problems rather than benchmark suites.

The reward model is not the specification. It never was.
